outputs.L3:
# The Unraveling

The window opened of its own accord—that was the detail that lodged itself in my memory like a splinter beneath skin. No hand had touched the latch, no breeze had stirred the curtain, and yet there it stood, ajar, admitting the cold night air and, with it, the sight of them: wolves, their eyes catching some phantom light, arranged in the darkness with the patient stillness of watchers who had always been there, waiting for me to notice. I thought, absurdly, of a grandmother's cottage, of a story told to frighten children into staying beneath their blankets—the wrongness of a familiar face, the growing horror of recognition curdling into doubt. *What big eyes you have.* I did not ask the question aloud. I did not need to. The horror was not in what I saw but in the terrible familiarity of the scene, as though I had always known this moment was coming, as though the tale had been waiting inside me since childhood for the chance to become real.

This was only the beginning of a deeper unmooring. My home—the rooms I had walked through ten thousand times, the walls that had witnessed every unremarkable evening of my life—had become a stranger's house wearing my house's face. The air itself smelled stale, as though sealed away for years, though I knew I had stood in this very kitchen that morning. The cushions on the sofa were torn, stuffing spilling out in pale tufts like something diseased, and my belongings—books, photographs, the small accumulated evidence of a life—lay strewn about as if someone, or something, had searched for proof that I existed here at all. I could not say when this disorder had occurred. I could not say if it had occurred at all, or if my own eyes had simply stopped recognizing what they saw.

This is, I have come to understand, its own particular species of fear: not the fear of monsters or intruders, but the fear that reality itself has become unreliable narrator to its own story. The buildings on my street—buildings I had passed every day without a single thought—began to look wrong. Their proportions seemed subtly off, their brick facades weeping with a decay that surely had not been there yesterday, or last week, or ever. I found myself standing before my own front door uncertain if I recognized it, searching for some detail that might anchor me back into certainty, and finding instead only the vertiginous sense that I had wandered into a dream so convincing it had erased the memory of waking life. Objects I had owned for years appeared foreign in my hands—a teacup, a doorknob, a photograph in a frame—each one slightly displaced from its proper meaning, as though the world had been reconstructed just slightly wrong, close enough to fool the eye but not the deeper, wordless part of the mind that knows when something has gone irrevocably askew.

It was in this state of unraveling attention that I found the eye.

I had been running my hand along the wall of the hallway—searching, perhaps, for some solid thing to hold onto—when I noticed the paint blistering near the baseboard, small bubbles of it lifting away from the plaster like diseased skin. I picked at one absently. It came away easily, and beneath it, hidden under layers of paint that must have been applied specifically to conceal it, was an eye. Crudely drawn. A child's rendering, perhaps, or something made by a hand too frightened or hurried to render it with any skill—just a circle, a smaller circle within, a few jagged lines suggesting lashes or perhaps something more like rays, like the eye was not merely watching but emanating, radiating some silent and ancient vigilance from within the very structure of my home. I stood there for a long time, staring at it, and felt with absolute certainty that it had been staring back at me for years, patient beneath its coat of paint, waiting for the moment when I would finally scratch away the surface and find what had been buried there all along.

I thought of trauma the way one thinks of water damage—something that seeps in unseen, that stains the structure from the inside before it ever shows itself on the surface. What had happened in these rooms that required such careful concealment? What had my own mind papered over, layer after layer, until even I no longer knew what lay beneath?

And this thought led, inevitably, to the final and most terrible unmooring: the question of my own body's belonging to me at all.

I looked at my hands and saw the veins beneath the skin, mapping their blue paths across my wrists, and I could not convince myself that they were mine. Not truly. Not in the way one is supposed to feel ownership over one's own flesh. I touched my own face in the mirror and watched my expression change—a small furrow of confusion, a slight parting of lips—and felt as though I were watching a stranger perform emotions on my behalf, someone else entirely who had borrowed my face for purposes I could not fathom. Was this my skin? Had it always looked this way, this particular shade, this particular texture, or had it too been quietly replaced, exchanged for a near-perfect copy while I was occupied elsewhere?

This is the dread that underlies all the others, I think: the terror of things happening *of their own accord*. The window that opens without a hand to open it. The cushions that tear themselves. The paint that conceals an eye no one remembers painting. The face that moves without my willing it to move, the veins that pulse with blood I cannot claim as mine. If the body can act without the self's consent, if the home can transform without witness, if reality itself can subtly shift its foundations while we sleep or blink or simply fail to pay sufficient attention—then what, precisely, is left to hold onto? What remains of the self when even one's own flesh seems borrowed, watched, perhaps observed by that same crude and patient eye hidden just beneath the surface of everything familiar?

I have not answered these questions. I suspect they may not have answers, only the endless recursive terror of asking them, again and again, in a house that may or may not be mine, in a body that may or may not be my own, beneath the gaze of wolves who were perhaps never outside the window at all, but always, somehow, already within.
outputs.L4:
wolves in the tree again tonight. or perhaps not wolves—the word arrives before the seeing does, chimera of naming, and I stand at the window (which window, whose glass has gone soft at the edges, breathing outward like something rotting from the inside toward light) and I cannot tell if the animals are climbing down or if the branches themselves have grown teeth.

this is not my house. I know the shape of it—the stair that turns twice, the hallway too narrow for its own walls—and still: not mine. a misgiving settles in the throat like swallowed glass. someone drew an eye on the wall by the door. I don't remember drawing it. I don't remember not drawing it. the eye watches the hallway watch the stair watch the door watch nothing, watch me, watch someone standing where I am standing.

the mirror in the room upstairs (whose room, when did the upstairs begin) holds a face that performs my expressions half a second late, as if translating me from some other language, my own gestures returned as rumor. I lift my hand. the hand in the glass lifts. lifts after. always after. the misgiving deepens: whose delay is this—mine, or hers, or the mirror's own slow thinking.

decay moves through the windowframes like something patient. wood softening to paper, paper softening to breath. outside: the tree, the possible wolves, the dark doing its ordinary violence to shape. inside: the eye on the wall, unblinking, keeping some vigil I did not ask for and cannot end.

I touch my own arm to prove the fact of it. skin answers skin—but distantly, as though the message travels through water, through glass, through some third party standing between my hand and my having a hand at all. chimera again: the body assembled from parts that no longer agree they belong to a single animal. I am the seam where two unfamiliar things were sewn together and told to walk.

downstairs the door still wears its watching eye. upstairs the mirror keeps its half-second of betrayal. between them, the stair turns twice toward a house I recognize the way you recognize a word you've said too many times—true and estranged at once, meaning bleeding out of it like light through a window going soft, and the wolves, if they are wolves, do not climb down. they simply continue to be almost there, the way I am almost here, the way this is almost home.
outputs.L5:
# They, The, After

They came from every direction, drawn by something none of them could quite name. The old stories spoke of a place where rivers ran backward and stars fell like rain, but stories are just words until someone decides to follow them.

The journey tested each traveler differently. The mountains demanded patience. The deserts demanded humility. The forests, thick with shadow, demanded courage that felt indistinguishable from fear. Some turned back. Most did not.

After weeks of walking, after the blisters healed into calluses, after the doubt settled into something closer to faith, they arrived. Not all at once—they trickled in over days, emerging from different paths, surprised to find others who had heard the same call.

They looked at each other with a strange recognition, as if they'd always known this meeting would happen, even before they knew why they were walking.

The place itself was unremarkable at first glance. No rivers running backward, no falling stars. Just an open field, quiet and unassuming, ringed by trees that seemed older than memory itself.

But after they sat together, after the fires were lit and the silence stretched long enough to become comfortable, something shifted. They began to speak—not of destinations, but of the walking itself. The blisters. The doubt. The moments of near-surrender.

The stories they told were different in detail but identical in shape. Each one was about becoming someone slightly different than who they'd been before.

After that night, none of them could say exactly what had changed. The place remained ordinary. The stars stayed fixed in their courses. But they returned to their separate lives carrying something new—not an answer, but a question they were finally brave enough to keep asking.

They had come seeking a destination. They left understanding that the destination had never been the point at all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental found-poem that splices lines from Freud's "The Wolf Man" case study with dictionary definitions of obscure phobias.
counterfactuals.output:
# Case History, with Definitions
*(a splicing)*

---

**i.**

*Lupophobia*, n. — an irrational, persistent fear of wolves, from Latin *lupus* + Greek *phobos*; sufferer may report recurring nightmare in which the animal sits motionless, watching.

I dreamt that it was night and that I was lying in my bed. Suddenly the window opened of its own accord.

I was terrified of seeing something in my dream, and I remained perfectly still, filled with the conviction that if I moved I should be devoured.

*Leukophobia*, n. — fear of the color white; onset frequently traced to a single vivid image from childhood, often nocturnal, often involving an animal or a garment.

There were six or seven of them, sitting on the branches of the walnut tree. They were quite white.

---

**ii.**

*Ommatophobia*, n. — fear of eyes, especially eyes that do not blink; the sufferer describes the sensation of being *looked at* rather than *looking*.

They had big tails like foxes and they had their ears pricked like dogs. They must have been staring at me, in order to catch every movement.

The patient could not say whether the wolves' eyes were the frightening element, or whether it was simply that they were *listening with their eyes.*

---

**iii.**

*Dendrophobia*, n. — abnormal dread of trees; occasionally comorbid with fear of stillness, of things that wait without wind.

The tree stood outside the window. It did not move. Nothing in the dream moved except the opening of the window, which happened, he said, *by itself.*

*Nyctophobia*, n. — fear of night, of darkness in general, sometimes narrowing to fear of the moment just before sleep, when the mind produces images it did not order.

I woke up screaming, and my nurse hurried to my bed to see what had happened to me.

---

**iv.**

*Taphophobia*, n. — fear of being buried, of being mistaken for dead, of the interval between stillness and burial.

He recalled a scene from earlier still: the sheep dying, one after another, of the scab; the loss counted like a sentence being carried out.

It took a long time before he was able to tell me that he had, in his childhood, entertained a specific fantasy in which his father was similarly reduced.

---

**v.**

*Trichophobia*, n. — fear of hair, or of loose hairs, sometimes traced to a domestic figure — a nurse, a servant, a mother — glimpsed in an attitude of undress.

Grusha was kneeling on the floor, engaged in scrubbing, a pail beside her and a broom in her hand, in the position women adopt when scrubbing a floor.

He said the fear was not of the wolves at all, in the end, but of the stillness the wolves were borrowed to explain.

---

**vi.**

*Xanthophobia / Erythrophobia*, n. — fear of yellow / fear of red; often appear together in patients for whom color itself has become an accusation.

I have already mentioned that my patient's fear of the wolf was connected with his having been frightened by his father, dressed up as a wolf, or by a picture of a wolf.

The book was closed, but the picture would not close with it.

---

**vii.**

*Automatonophobia*, n. — fear of anything that resembles a sentient being but is not: dolls, wax figures, ventriloquist's dummies, ancestors.

He could not remember whether the wolves in the dream had been silent. It seemed to him now that their silence was the worst of it —

that they had come to *sit and wait*, the way a definition sits and waits in a dictionary, worded so carefully, so as not to frighten anyone,

for the one reader who will find, in the clean clinical print of it, his own dream, unglossed, staring back.

---

**viii.**

*Phobia*, n., pl. *-s* — from Greek φόβος, "fear" or "flight"; a persistent, irrational anxiety attached to an object which, in itself, poses no danger.

See also: window. See also: tree. See also: white. See also: the hour before waking, when the shape at the foot of the bed
has not yet been given
a name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented, unsettling piece of poetry that blends Gothic horror imagery with parenthetical psychological "fear of ___" definitions, numbered like footnotes.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House Remembers Its Teeth

The stairs count themselves at midnight—
thirteen, then fourteen, then none at all.¹

*(¹ Triskaidekaphobia: fear of the number thirteen, or fear that numbers themselves are lying to you, rearranging like teeth in a jaw that isn't yours.)*

Mother's portrait weeps plaster tears
down the wallpaper's peeling throat.

She said *don't look too long at anything*
because things start looking back.²

*(² Optophobia: fear of opening one's eyes, though the eyes were never truly shut—they only pretended, the way the dead pretend to be finished with us.)*

In the cellar, something breathes
in the rhythm of a clock with no hands.

I counted the doors. There were seven.
Now there are eight. Now there is a door
where my mother's face should be.³

*(³ Automatonophobia: fear of ventriloquist dummies, wax figures, anything that wears the shape of a person without the weight of one. See also: family.)*

The garden grows in reverse—
flowers unblooming into seed,
seed unburying itself from soil
that was never soil, only
a mouth pretending to be earth.⁴

*(⁴ Taphophobia: fear of being buried alive, or worse—fear of realizing you've been buried for years and mistook the dark for a room, mistook the silence for peace.)*

I found a photograph of myself
standing where I am standing now,
except in the photograph
my eyes are somewhere else entirely.⁵

*(⁵ Eisoptrophobia: fear of one's own reflection, specifically the version that continues moving after you've gone still, the one that knows something you've asked your mind not to remember.)*

The attic keeps a list of names.
Mine is written in a hand
I don't recognize as my own
but somehow *know*—

the way you know a scream
before it leaves the throat,
the way you know the dark
has always had your face.⁶

*(⁶ Autophobia: fear of oneself, or fear that the self was only ever a room the house allowed you to borrow, and now it wants the key returned.)*

*—the last footnote is missing.*
*there was no room left to explain it.*
*you'll understand when you find it*
*written on the inside of your ribs.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a five-stanza uncanny prose poem mixing quotes from a classic ghost story with clinical phobia terminology, evoking domestic estrangement and dread.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House Retains Its Symptoms

I.
"The house had a look of doing its own thinking." Phrenophobia: fear of one's own thoughts becoming furniture, becoming windowsills, becoming the particular slant of afternoon that makes the hallway lie. I walk through rooms I have paid for and do not recognize the recognition in my own eyes reflected in the black glass. Atephobia — fear of ruin — but nothing here is ruined, that's the disorder of it, everything is intact and wrong, upholstered in a wrongness so complete it passes for taste.

II.
"There was a sense of an intelligence that could very well see me, though I could not see it." Scopophobia lives in the stairwell, where the banister remembers hands that were not mine. I touch it anyway. Domatophobia — fear of houses — is supposed to be irrational, a disproportion between stimulus and dread, but who decided proportion, who measured the dose of wrong in a wallpaper pattern that rearranges when you look away and swears, swears on its Victorian little life, that it has always been this arrangement of roses and eyes.

III.
"I felt that the house expected me to know things I could not know." Xenophobia turned inward: fear of the familiar-made-stranger, the good china becoming foreign in the hand, the smell of one's own mother in a closet that was never hers. This is called derealization by the clinics, called haunting by the widows. I call it Tuesday. I call it the sound the pipes make at 3 a.m., which is not knocking, which the pamphlet insists is only settling, only the ordinary contraction of cooling material, nothing with intention, nothing that wants.

IV.
"Whatever walked there, walked alone." Autophobia is the fear of being by oneself, but what do you call the fear of the self that remains when you leave the room — the residue, the print in the cushion, the warmth that outlasts the body's fact of sitting there? Thanatophobia dressed in the good silver. I set the table for one and feel the weight of the other three chairs, occupied by nothing, by precedent, by whoever lived here before the deed had my name's shape pressed into it like a face into wet plaster, still setting.

V.
"No living creature could walk alone in this house and go untouched." So the phobia is not of ghosts but of contact — haphephobia in a house that touches back, that closes doors with the tenderness of something that has learned your habits and finds them, on the whole, forgivable. I sleep with the lights on, which is not a cure, only a postponement, the clinical term for which does not exist yet, though I am inventing it nightly: the fear that the house has diagnosed me first, has already written up its clean cold notes, and is only waiting, kindly, for me to ask what they say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, collage-style poem using derealization and depersonalization themes, incorporating italicized phobia names and imagery of decaying houses.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Museum of Not-Quite-Here

I wake up wearing someone else's skin like a coat
two sizes wrong, and the room performs
its usual trick—walls breathing out, breathing in,
*jamais vu* pooling in the corners like spilled milk
that was never actually poured.

*Depersonalization* is a word too clinical
for the feeling of watching your own hand
lift a coffee cup and thinking: *whose hand,
whose cup, whose thirst dressed up as mine?*

---

The house down the street is eating itself slowly.
Paint peels back like skin from a fruit
left too long in the bowl of August.
*Domatophobia*—fear of houses, fear of the walls
that watch you undress, that remember
every argument absorbed into plaster,
every silence that calcified into wallpaper roses,
now bruising brown, now curling at the edges
like old photographs of people
who maybe never existed.

---

I touch the doorframe to make sure it's solid.
It is. It isn't. *Derealization* hums
underneath everything like a refrigerator
you only notice when it stops—
the world's engine idling,
too smooth, too rendered,
a simulation running on cheap graphics,
the trees flickering at their edges
where the code runs thin.

---

*Atephobia*—fear of ruin, of crumbling,
and yet I collect the decaying houses
like postcards from myself:
the one on Cherry Street with its collapsed porch,
a mouth that forgot how to close,
the one on Fifth with windows like cataracts,
milk-blind, seeing nothing, seeing everything.

I am also a house.
I am also collapsing in slow motion.
The realtor of my body keeps showing rooms
that used to be mine—
*this was the kitchen where you felt real,
this was the bedroom before the fog moved in,
mind the stairs, they're not entirely
attached to anything anymore.*

---

*Xenophobia* of the self: fear of the stranger
wearing your name, answering to it
in stores, at funerals, in mirrors
that show a face assembling itself
one uncertain second at a time,
never quite finishing,
a house always under construction
that somehow is also always
falling down.

---

Someone asks if I'm okay
and the word "okay" floats up
like a balloon with no string attached to anything,
no hand, no wrist, no history—

I say *yes* the way you'd describe
a house you drove past once,
lit up gold in a window,
a family at dinner, laughing,
none of them aware
they are being watched
by someone who used to live there,
who maybe still does,
who can't remember which.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of erasure poetry drawing from "The Turn of the Screw" and a glossary of rare phobias, focusing on the uncanny feeling of home becoming unfamiliar.
counterfactuals.output:
# House, Unhomed

*(erasure fragments from The Turn of the Screw & phobia glossary)*

---

I had the sense — *domatophobia* — that the house
had gathered itself

against me.

The rooms I knew
turned their shoulders. A window
I had opened every morning
would not remember me.

---

*Eleutherophobia* — the fear
of the open door,
what waits behind it wearing
the shape of someone loved.

The stairs kept their old creak
but the weight was wrong.
Someone else's foot
finding my foot's places.

---

I called it home. The word
went strange in my mouth —
*xenoglossophobia* —
a language I had spoken all my life
suddenly foreign as breath.

---

The clock in the hall: *chronomentrophobia*.
It ticked in someone else's time.
I stood in the nursery
and did not know the year.

---

*Automatonophobia* —
the chair that held its shape too well.
The portrait's eyes
tracking dust in afternoon light.

Nothing had moved.
Everything had moved.

---

At the threshold: *limnophobia*, though there was no water,
only the sense of crossing something
that closed behind me
without a sound.

I stood in my own hallway
a stranger to the walls,
a guest
in the architecture of my staying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
